claim: Proteasomes are central regulators of protein homeostasis in eukaryotes.
source: Proteasomes are central regulators of protein homeostasis in eukaryotes.
evidence: This is established scientific knowledge about proteasome function in eukaryotic cells.

claim: Reducing expression of individual subunits of the proteasome's 19S regulatory complex increased survival when flux through the proteasome was reduced to the point of toxicity.
source: Counter to expectation, reducing expression of individual subunits of the proteasome's 19S regulatory complex increased survival.
evidence: This claim is supported by the genome-wide screen results showing enrichment of 19S subunit gene insertions in cells surviving proteasome inhibitor treatment.

claim: Strong 19S reduction was cytotoxic but modest reduction protected cells from inhibitors.
source: Strong 19S reduction was cytotoxic but modest reduction protected cells from inhibitors.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data showing that complete knockout was lethal but partial knockdown increased resistance.

claim: Protection from proteasome inhibitors was accompanied by an increased ratio of 20S to 26S proteasomes.
source: Protection was accompanied by an increased ratio of 20S to 26S proteasomes, preservation of protein degradation capacity and reduced proteotoxic stress.
evidence: This is supported by native gel analysis showing increased 20S and decreased 26S proteasomes in protected cells.

claim: Protection from proteasome inhibitors was accompanied by preservation of protein degradation capacity.
source: Protection was accompanied by an increased ratio of 20S to 26S proteasomes, preservation of protein degradation capacity and reduced proteotoxic stress.
evidence: This is supported by protein degradation assays showing maintained degradation rates in 19S knockdown cells treated with bortezomib.

claim: Protection from proteasome inhibitors was accompanied by reduced proteotoxic stress.
source: Protection was accompanied by an increased ratio of 20S to 26S proteasomes, preservation of protein degradation capacity and reduced proteotoxic stress.
evidence: This is supported by RNA-seq data showing reduced stress response gene expression and reduced polyubiquitinated protein accumulation.

claim: The mechanism of rebalancing proteostasis through 19S compromise is conserved from yeast to humans.
source: This means of rebalancing proteostasis is conserved from yeast to humans.
evidence: This is supported by experiments showing that yeast DAmP strains with reduced 19S subunits also showed increased resistance to MG132.

claim: Perturbation of protein homeostasis is central to diverse human diseases.
source: The importance of these systems is underscored by the fact that perturbation of protein homeostasis is central to diverse human diseases (Balch et al., 2008; Labbadia and Morimoto, 2015).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior literature.

claim: In neurodegenerative diseases, cells succumb to an overload of toxic protein aggregates.
source: In neurodegenerative diseases, cells succumb to an overload of toxic protein aggregates.
evidence: This is established knowledge about neurodegenerative disease mechanisms.

claim: In cancer, malignant cells co-opt protein quality control systems to accommodate severe proteotoxic stresses.
source: Whereas in cancer, malignant cells co-opt protein quality control systems to accommodate the severe proteotoxic stresses that arise from high mutation loads, relentless biomass accumulation and protein turnover (Mendillo et al., 2012; Deshaies, 2014; Scherz-Shouval et al., 2014).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior literature.

claim: Cells are highly vulnerable to insults that impair the function of the ubiquitin-proteasome system.
source: Because the ubiquitin-proteasome system is the major mechanism regulating protein turnover, cells are highly vulnerable to insults that impair the function of this system (Varshavsky, 2012; Petrocca et al., 2013).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior literature.

claim: Misfolded and aggregated proteins can bind the proteasome and stabilize an inactive closed conformation.
source: Such proteins can bind the proteasome and stabilize an inactive closed conformation (Deriziotis et al., 2011; Ayyadevara et al., 2015).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior literature.

claim: Chemically diverse natural product inhibitors of the ubiquitin-proteasome pathway are elaborated by organisms as diverse as terrestrial and marine bacteria, fungi, and plants.
source: In addition, chemically diverse natural product inhibitors of the ubiquitin-proteasome pathway are elaborated by organisms as diverse as terrestrial and marine bacteria, fungi, and plants (Kisselev et al., 2006; Schneekloth and Crews, 2011; Kisselev et al., 2012).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior literature.

claim: Proteasome inhibitors can thwart the proliferation of neighboring organisms and thereby provide a competitive growth advantage.
source: These proteasome inhibitors can thwart the proliferation of neighboring organisms and thereby provide a competitive growth advantage.
evidence: This is an inference based on the ecological role of proteasome inhibitors produced by microorganisms.

claim: Malignant cells in which the rates of protein synthesis outstrip proteasome degradation capacity are exceedingly vulnerable to proteasome inhibition.
source: Malignant cells in which the rates of protein synthesis outstrip proteasome degradation capacity are exceedingly vulnerable to proteasome inhibition (Adams et al., 2000; Cenci et al., 2012; Deshaies, 2014).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior literature.

claim: Bortezomib is broadly applied as a therapy for patients with myeloma or mantle cell lymphoma.
source: Indeed, it is broadly applied as a therapy for patients with myeloma or mantle cell lymphoma (Chen et al., 2011; Crawford and Irvine, 2013).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior literature about clinical applications.

claim: The 26S proteasome is comprised of a 20S catalytic core and a 19S regulatory complex that can be attached to either or both ends of the 20S core.
source: This complex is comprised of a 20S catalytic core that orchestrates peptide bond cleavage and a 19S regulatory complex that can be attached to either or both ends of the 20S core (Besche et al., 2009; Matyskiela et al., 2013; Tomko and Hochstrasser, 2013).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior literature describing proteasome structure.

claim: The 19S complex recognizes ubiquitin-tagged substrates, cleaves ubiquitin chains, unfolds substrates and translocates the unfolded proteins into the catalytic chamber of the 20S core.
source: The 19S complex recognizes ubiquitin-tagged substrates, cleaves ubiquitin chains, unfolds substrates and translocates the unfolded proteins into the catalytic chamber of the 20S core (Hochstrasser, 1996; Finley, 2009; Matyskiela et al., 2013).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior literature describing 19S complex function.

claim: Pre-existing intrinsic resistance and acquired resistance following drug exposure have limited the effectiveness of bortezomib as a therapeutic.
source: Such an understanding is of great importance in the dynamics of natural ecosystems in the face of diverse proteotoxic stresses and in the clinic, where pre-existing intrinsic resistance and acquired resistance following drug exposure have limited the effectiveness of bortezomib as a therapeutic.
evidence: This is established knowledge about clinical challenges with bortezomib therapy.

claim: Bortezomib and MG132 inhibit both 20S and 26S proteasomes by targeting the core proteolytic catalytic activity of the 20S subunits.
source: These inhibit both 20S and 26S proteasomes by targeting the core proteolytic catalytic activity of the 20S subunits (Kisselev et al., 2006, 2012; Goldberg, 2012).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior literature describing the mechanism of action of these inhibitors.

claim: A library of 100 million gene-trap insertions in near-haploid human KBM7 cells was used to screen for resistance to proteasome inhibitors.
source: We used these inhibitors at toxic levels in an unbiased, genome-wide screen. We selected for cells that were resistant to the inhibitors from a library of 100 million gene-trap insertions, using a human cell line that is haploid for all chromosomes except chromosome 8 (Carette et al., 2009, 2011a).
evidence: This describes the experimental methodology used in the study.

claim: For the MG132 resistance screen, 992 independent insertion sites were identified in the pool of surviving cells.
source: For the MG132 resistance screen, we identified 992 independent insertion sites in the pool of surviving cells.
evidence: This is a direct result from the screening experiment.

claim: All insertions that reached a high level of statistical enrichment (p-value < 1 e−7) in the MG132 screen lay in genes encoding subunits of the proteasome 19S regulatory complex.
source: Surprisingly, all insertions that reached a high level of statistical enrichment (p-value < 1 e−7) lay in genes encoding subunits of the proteasome 19S regulatory complex (Figure 1B,C; Supplementary file 1).
evidence: This is supported by the screening data presented in Figure 1B,C and Supplementary file 1.

claim: 19S subunit genes enriched in the MG132 screen included both ATPase subunits (PSMC2, PSMC3, PSMC4, PSMC5, and PSMC6) and non-ATPase subunits (PSMD2, PSMD6, PSMD7, and PSMD12).
source: These included both ATPase subunits (PSMC2, PSMC3, PSMC4, PSMC5, and PSMC6) as well as non-ATPase subunits (PSMD2, PSMD6, PSMD7, and PSMD12).
evidence: This is a direct result from the screening experiment.

claim: No insertions were recovered in genes encoding subunits of the 20S catalytic core in the MG132 screen.
source: No insertions were recovered in genes encoding subunits of the 20S catalytic core (Supplementary file 1).
evidence: This is a direct result from the screening experiment.

claim: For the bortezomib resistance screen, 538 independent insertions were recovered.
source: For the bortezomib resistance screen, we recovered 538 independent insertions.
evidence: This is a direct result from the screening experiment.

claim: Seven of the ten most highly enriched genes in the bortezomib screen encoded subunits of the 19S complex.
source: The results of the 2 screens were remarkably similar with seven of the ten most highly enriched genes encoding subunits of the 19S complex (Supplementary file 1).
evidence: This is a direct result from the screening experiment.

claim: Stable clones containing 19S subunit gene insertions could not be isolated from the resistant pools of cells.
source: From the resistant pools of cells, we then attempted to isolate stable clones that contained 19S subunit gene insertions. We were unable to do so.
evidence: This is a direct experimental observation.

claim: Targeted deletion of PSMD12 in HAP1 cells using CRISPR only recovered diploid cell variants in which just one of the two PSMD12 alleles was disrupted.
source: Next, we attempted to delete PSMD12 in a near-haploid fibroblast cell line (HAP1) (Carette et al., 2010; Essletzbichler et al., 2014). With this targeted approach using CRISPR constructs, we were only able to recover diploid cell variants in which just one of the two PSMD12 alleles was disrupted.
evidence: This is a direct experimental observation.

claim: Cre-mediated inversion of gene-trap cassettes in PSMC2 or PSMD12 genes in mouse embryonic stem cells resulted in less than 1% cell survival.
source: We induced Cre-mediated inversion in over 3000 cells harboring each cassette, but less than 1% of the cells survived.
evidence: This is a direct experimental observation.

claim: All stable clones that emerged after Cre-mediated inversion retained expression of the targeted 19S subunits.
source: We confirmed that inversion had occurred in the surviving cells. However, all of the stable clones that emerged retained expression of the targeted subunits (Figure 1—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1.

claim: The function of the 19S regulatory complex is essential for sustained proliferation of mammalian cells under basal conditions.
source: These findings confirm that, as others have found in yeast and Drosophila, the function of the 19S regulatory complex is essential for sustained proliferation of mammalian cells under basal conditions.
evidence: This is inferred from the inability to generate stable complete knockouts and is consistent with prior literature in other organisms.

claim: Cells carrying 19S mutations became enriched in the initial screens because they provided cells with a short-term advantage for growth over several generations.
source: Presumably, cells carrying 19S mutations had become enriched in our initial MG132 and bortezomib screens because they provided cells with a short-term advantage for growth over several generations.
evidence: This is an inference based on the screening results and the inability to isolate stable clones.

claim: A panel of shRNA-expressing lentiviruses targeting seventeen 19S subunits and three 20S subunits was assembled.
source: We assembled a panel of shRNA-expressing lentiviruses targeting seventeen 19S subunits and three 20S subunits (PSMB5, PSMB7, and PSMA3).
evidence: This describes the experimental methodology.

claim: Knockdown of any of the subunits of the 20S catalytic core reduced viability with or without bortezomib.
source: With or without bortezomib, knockdown of any of the subunits of the 20S catalytic core reduced viability (Figure 2A, Figure 2—figure supplement 1A–D).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2A and Figure 2—figure supplement 1A–D.

claim: Knockdown of several different 19S subunits had opposing effects on viability depending on the absence or presence of bortezomib.
source: In contrast, the effects of knocking down several different 19S subunits had opposing effects, depending on the absence or presence of the inhibitor. In its absence, 19S subunit reduction had a fitness cost and decreased cell viability; in its presence, 19S subunit reduction provided a survival advantage and increased viability (Figure 2A, Figure 2—figure supplement 1A–D).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2A and Figure 2—figure supplement 1A–D.

claim: Two cell lines with stable expression of shRNA targeting either PSMC5 or PSMD2 had only a modest reduction in protein levels and proliferated normally.
source: Long-term 19S subunit reduction impeded the growth of most cells, but we were able to propagate two lines that proliferated normally (Figure 2—figure supplement 1E). These lines stably expressed shRNA targeting either PSMC5 or PSMD2. In both cases, the lines had only a modest reduction in protein levels (Figure 2—figure supplement 1F).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1E,F.

claim: Cells with reduced PSMC5 or PSMD2 continued proliferating at a concentration of bortezomib (12 nM) that completely inhibited the proliferation of control cells.
source: At a concentration of bortezomib that completely inhibited the proliferation of control cells (12 nM), these cells continued proliferating (Figure 2B, figure 2—figure supplement 1G).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2B and Figure 2—figure supplement 1G.

claim: In cells with reduced levels of either PSMC5 or PSMD2, 26S proteasome complexes were reduced and 20S proteasome complexes were increased.
source: In cells with reduced levels of either PSMC5 or PSMD2, 26S proteasome complexes were reduced and 20S proteasome complexes were increased (Figure 2C, upper panel).
evidence: This is supported by native gel analysis shown in Figure 2C.

claim: Changes in proteasome complex ratios persisted in the presence of bortezomib in cells with reduced PSMC5 or PSMD2.
source: These changes persisted in the presence of bortezomib (Figure 2C).
evidence: This is supported by native gel analysis shown in Figure 2C.

claim: Exposing control cells to 12 nM bortezomib for 24 hr led to a nearly complete inactivation of 20S proteasome function.
source: Exposing control cells to 12 nM bortezomib for 24 hr led to a nearly complete inactivation of 20S proteasome function (Figure 2C, lower panel).
evidence: This is supported by proteasome activity assay shown in Figure 2C.

claim: Cells with reduced levels of either PSMC5 or PSMD2 maintained a significant level of 20S proteasome activity after bortezomib treatment.
source: Cells with reduced levels of either PSMC5 or PSMD2 maintained a significant level of 20S proteasome activity (Figure 2C).
evidence: This is supported by proteasome activity assay shown in Figure 2C.

claim: Four additional cell lines with different shRNAs driving modest reduction in PSMD2 protein levels were all significantly more resistant to bortezomib than the parental line.
source: To validate our findings, we selected four additional cell lines each with a different shRNA driving modest reduction in PSMD2 protein levels. Again, all of these lines were significantly more resistant to bortezomib than the parental line (EC50 values increased by three to sixfold, Figure 2D).
evidence: This is supported by dose-response data shown in Figure 2D.

claim: In cells with reduced PSMD2, 26S proteasome complexes were reduced and both the levels and the activity of 20S proteasome complexes were sharply increased.
source: In these cells, we also observed that 26S proteasome complexes were reduced and that both the levels and the activity of 20S proteasome complexes were sharply increased (Figure 2E).
evidence: This is supported by native gel and activity assay data shown in Figure 2E.

claim: In the presence of bortezomib, reducing 19S subunits enabled the relative preservation of the levels and activity of 20S proteasome complexes.
source: Notably, in the presence of bortezomib, reducing 19S subunits enabled the relative preservation of the levels and activity of 20S proteasome complexes (Figure 2E).
evidence: This is supported by native gel and activity assay data shown in Figure 2E.

claim: In four cell lines with modest reductions of PSMD2, NRF1 was not constitutively activated.
source: Surprisingly, in the four cell lines with modest reductions of PSMD2, we did not detect constitutive activation of NRF1, and correspondingly, the expression of 20S subunits was unaltered (Figure 2F).
evidence: This is supported by Western blot data shown in Figure 2F.

claim: HSF1 was not activated in cells with modest reductions of PSMD2 as reflected by the stable expression of HSP70.
source: Moreover, HSF1 was not activated as reflected by the stable expression of HSP70, the protein that is most highly responsive to proteotoxic stress (Figure 2F).
evidence: This is supported by Western blot data shown in Figure 2F.

claim: Polyubiquitinated proteins did not accumulate in the PSMD2 knockdown cells under basal conditions.
source: Consistent with these findings, polyubiquitinated proteins did not accumulate in the PSMD2 knockdown cells (Figure 2F) suggesting that modestly reducing 19S subunit levels did not itself induce a cytoprotective stress response.
evidence: This is supported by Western blot data shown in Figure 2F.

claim: The accumulation of polyubiquitinated proteins was reduced in cells with reduced PSMD2 levels relative to control cells treated with bortezomib.
source: Not only were stress response pathways not activated, but the response to bortezomib was blunted in cells with reduced PSMD2 levels. The accumulation of polyubiquitinated proteins was reduced relative to control cells treated with the inhibitor.
evidence: This is inferred from the Western blot data showing reduced ubiquitin accumulation.

claim: The activation of NRF1 was reduced in cells with reduced PSMD2 levels following bortezomib treatment.
source: The activation of NRF1 was also reduced (Figure 2F).
evidence: This is supported by Western blot data shown in Figure 2F.

claim: The protective effect of 19S subunit reduction was specific to the toxicity caused by proteasome inhibitors.
source: Notably, the protective effect of 19S subunit reduction was specific to the toxicity caused by proteasome inhibitors.
evidence: This is supported by data showing that cells with reduced PSMD2 remained sensitive to other stressors.

claim: Cells with reduced PSMD2 levels remained fully sensitive to small molecule mediators of ER stress, HSP90 inhibition, thiol adduct formation or blockade of translation initiation or translation elongation.
source: Cells with reduced PSMD2 levels remained fully sensitive to small molecule mediators of ER stress, HSP90 inhibition, thiol adduct formation or blockade of translation initiation or translation elongation among other stresses (Figure 2—figure supplement 1I–N).
evidence: This is supported by dose-response data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1I–N.

claim: Modest 19S subunit reduction protected cells by selectively lowering the proteotoxic stress that is generated by proteasome inhibition.
source: Thus, modest 19S subunit reduction protected cells by selectively lowering the proteotoxic stress that is generated by proteasome inhibition.
evidence: This is an inference based on the specificity of protection and the reduced stress response.

claim: Whole-genome RNA-sequencing was performed in two lines with modest reductions in PSMD2.
source: To examine in detail the transcriptional changes that characterize cells with increased resistance to proteasome inhibition, we performed whole-genome RNA-sequencing in two lines with modest reductions in PSMD2.
evidence: This describes the experimental methodology.

claim: PSMD2 mRNA levels were reduced by approximately 50% in both cell lines used for RNA-sequencing.
source: Sequence data confirmed that PSMD2 mRNA levels were reduced by ∼50% in both lines.
evidence: This is a direct result from the RNA-sequencing experiment.

claim: Under basal conditions, cells with reduction in PSMD2 showed a strong induction of components of the ribosome.
source: Under basal conditions (in the absence of bortezomib), cells with reduction in PSMD2 showed a strong induction of components of the ribosome (gene set enrichment analysis false discovery rate [FDR] q-value = 4.0 e−22) (Supplementary file 3).
evidence: This is supported by gene set enrichment analysis of RNA-seq data.

claim: Genes encoding the 20S subunits of the proteasome were not induced in cells with PSMD2 reduction under basal conditions.
source: Genes encoding the 20S subunits of the proteasome were not induced, consistent with our earlier observation that NRF1 is not activated and 20S subunit levels are unchanged (Figure 2F).
evidence: This is supported by RNA-seq data and is consistent with Western blot data.

claim: The most strongly downregulated gene category in cells with PSMD2 reduction involved components of diverse proteotoxic stress responses.
source: The most strongly downregulated gene category involved components of diverse proteotoxic stress responses (FDR q-value = 2.31 e−9) (Supplementary file 3).
evidence: This is supported by gene set enrichment analysis of RNA-seq data.

claim: Downregulated stress response genes in PSMD2 knockdown cells included genes for sentinel proteins that respond to heat-shock, oxidative stress, and ER stress.
source: These included genes for sentinel proteins that respond to heat-shock (e.g., HSPA1A, HSPA1B, HSPA8, HSPB1, and HSP90AA1), oxidative stress (e.g., HMOX1), and ER stress (e.g., CHOP/DDIT3, TRIB3, and HERPUD1) (Figure 3A).
evidence: This is supported by RNA-seq data shown in Figure 3A.

claim: Genes previously identified as an HSF1-regulated cancer-specific transcriptional program were downregulated in PSMD2 knockdown cells.
source: Genes previously identified as an HSF1-regulated cancer-specific transcriptional program were also downregulated (Mendillo et al., 2012; Santagata et al., 2013) (FDR q-value = 0.042; normalized enrichment score (NES) 1.57) (Figure 3—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: This is supported by gene set enrichment analysis of RNA-seq data shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 1A.

claim: 19S subunit reduction not only fails to induce classic adaptive stress responses, but actually lowers basal levels of proteotoxic stress.
source: Therefore, 19S subunit reduction not only fails to induce classic adaptive stress responses, but actually lowers basal levels of proteotoxic stress.
evidence: This is an inference based on the RNA-seq data showing reduced stress response gene expression.

claim: In control cells, bortezomib treatment unleashed a powerful transcriptional response characterized by a sharp increase in stress-response transcripts.
source: As expected, in control cells, bortezomib treatment unleashed a powerful transcriptional response characterized by a sharp increase in stress-response transcripts (FDR q-value = 7.07 e−13) (Supplementary file 3).
evidence: This is supported by RNA-seq data.

claim: The potent bortezomib-induced stress response was markedly attenuated in cells with reduced PSMD2 levels.
source: This potent bortezomib-induced stress response was markedly attenuated in cells with reduced PSMD2 levels (Figure 3B).
evidence: This is supported by RNA-seq data shown in Figure 3B.

claim: The suppressed genes in PSMD2 knockdown cells following bortezomib treatment include ones involved in oxidative stress and ER stress responses, as well as genes in the HSF1-mediated heat-shock response.
source: The suppressed genes include ones involved in oxidative stress and ER stress responses, as well as genes in the HSF1-mediated heat-shock response (FDR q-value < 0.01; NES 2.317) (Figure 3B,C and Figure 3—figure supplement 1B).
evidence: This is supported by RNA-seq data and gene set enrichment analysis shown in Figure 3B,C and Figure 3—figure supplement 1B.

claim: Induction of HSP70 family heat-shock genes HSPA1A and HSPA1B was reduced by eightfold in PSMD2 knockdown cells following bortezomib treatment.
source: For example, induction of HSP70 family heat-shock genes HSPA1A and HSPA1B was reduced by eightfold, while HSPA6 was entirely suppressed (Figure 3B).
evidence: This is supported by RNA-seq data shown in Figure 3B.

claim: Previous work has identified 28 mediators of bortezomib toxicity, many of which are upregulated upon bortezomib exposure.
source: Previous work has identified 28 mediators of bortezomib toxicity, many of which are upregulated upon bortezomib exposure (Chen et al., 2010).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to prior literature.

claim: When control cells were treated with bortezomib, the mRNA transcripts of many bortezomib toxicity mediators increased significantly.
source: When we treated control cells with bortezomib, the mRNA transcripts of many of these genes increased significantly (e.g., ATG4A, DDX27, GADD45A, NUP54, ODC1, PMAIP1/NOXA, SETX, SNIP1, and TAX1BP1) (Supplementary file 3).
evidence: This is supported by RNA-seq data.

claim: The upregulation of bortezomib toxicity mediators was strongly attenuated in cells with reduced PSMD2 levels.
source: This response was also strongly attenuated in cells with reduced PSMD2 levels (Figure 3C,D, and Figure 3—figure supplement 1C).
evidence: This is supported by RNA-seq data shown in Figure 3C,D and Figure 3—figure supplement 1C.

claim: Selectively compromising 19S subunit expression broadly reduces the diverse transcriptional responses that normally ensue when flux through the proteasome is reduced.
source: Overall, selectively compromising 19S subunit expression broadly reduces the diverse transcriptional responses that normally ensue when flux through the proteasome is reduced.
evidence: This is an inference based on the comprehensive RNA-seq analysis.

claim: Cluster analysis on genes displaying the highest differential expression confirmed that PSMD2 reduction strongly blunted the bortezomib-mediated induction of stress response genes.
source: To further characterize the transcriptional effects of 19S subunit reduction, we performed a cluster analysis on the genes displaying the highest differential expression in our RNA-seq experiment (Figure 3E). This analysis confirmed that PSMD2 reduction strongly blunted the bortezomib-mediated induction of stress response genes (FDR q-values 1.2 e−5 to 1.2 e−13).
evidence: This is supported by cluster analysis of RNA-seq data shown in Figure 3E.

claim: In cells with reduced levels of PSMD2, bortezomib treatment strongly repressed genes involved in DNA replication and cell cycle control.
source: One group of genes highlighted by this analysis revealed a connection between the suppression of the cell cycle and increased resistance to bortezomib. In cells with reduced levels of PSMD2, bortezomib treatment strongly repressed genes involved in DNA replication (FDR q-value = 1.4 e−32) and cell cycle control (FDR q-value = 1.8 e−90).
evidence: This is supported by gene set enrichment analysis of RNA-seq data.

claim: The accentuated anti-proliferation response suggests that cells with reduced 19S subunits are primed to enter a protected, quiescent-like state when flux through the proteasome is compromised.
source: This accentuated anti-proliferation response suggests that cells with reduced 19S subunits are primed to enter a protected, quiescent-like state when flux through the proteasome is compromised.
evidence: This is an inference based on the transcriptional changes observed in RNA-seq data.

claim: A cell line was developed in which a PSMD2-targeting shRNA is transiently expressed from a doxycycline-regulated promoter.
source: To model the effects of transient reduction of 19S subunits, we developed a cell line in which a PSMD2-targeting shRNA is transiently expressed from a doxycycline-regulated promoter (Figure 4).
evidence: This describes the experimental methodology shown in Figure 4.

claim: Transient reduction of PSMD2 significantly increased resistance to both bortezomib and MG132.
source: The effects of transient reduction of PSMD2 mirrored the effects of stable PSMD2 reduction. Most notably, it significantly increased resistance to both bortezomib (Figure 4B, Figure 4—figure supplement 1A) and MG132 (Figure 4—figure supplement 1B).
evidence: This is supported by dose-response data shown in Figure 4B and Figure 4—figure supplement 1A,B.

claim: The resistance conferred by transient PSMD2 reduction was selective, and not accompanied by increased resistance to other small molecule stressors.
source: Again, this resistance was selective, and not accompanied by increased resistance to other small molecule stressors (Figure 4—figure supplement 1C–F).
evidence: This is supported by dose-response data shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 1C–F.

claim: In the absence of bortezomib, transient 19S reduction did not activate NRF1 or HSF1.
source: In the absence of bortezomib, transient 19S reduction did not activate NRF1 or HSF1 (Figure 4C)
evidence: This is supported by Western blot data shown in Figure 4C.

claim: Transient 19S reduction reduced activation of NRF1 and HSF1 following bortezomib exposure.
source: and reduced activation of NRF1 and HSF1 following bortezomib exposure (Figure 4C).
evidence: This is supported by Western blot data shown in Figure 4C.

claim: Transient reduction of PSMD2 increased the ratio of 20S/26S proteasomes and total levels of 20S proteasome activity.
source: Transient reduction of this 19S subunit increased the ratio of 20S/26S proteasomes and total levels of 20S proteasome activity (Figure 4D,E)
evidence: This is supported by native gel and glycerol gradient data shown in Figure 4D,E.

claim: Transient reduction of PSMD2 did not increase total levels of 20S subunits.
source: without increasing total levels of 20S subunits (Figure 4C, Figure 4—figure supplement 1G,H).
evidence: This is supported by Western blot data shown in Figure 4C and Figure 4—figure supplement 1G,H.

claim: Transient 19S subunit reduction preserved a fraction of the 20S proteasome complexes following bortezomib treatment and a corresponding portion of their activity remained.
source: Similar to the results we obtained in stable knockdown cells (Figure 2E), transient 19S subunit reduction preserved a fraction of the 20S proteasome complexes following bortezomib treatment and a corresponding portion of their activity remained (Figure 4D,E, Figure 4—figure supplement 1G,H).
evidence: This is supported by native gel and glycerol gradient data shown in Figure 4D,E and Figure 4—figure supplement 1G,H.

claim: In the absence of bortezomib, transiently reducing PSMD2 lowered rates of proteolysis by the lysosome but did not affect protein degradation by the proteasome.
source: In the absence of bortezomib, transiently reducing PSMD2 lowered rates of proteolysis by the lysosome (Figure 4—figure supplement 1I), but it did not affect protein degradation by the proteasome (Figure 4F).
evidence: This is supported by protein degradation assay data shown in Figure 4F and Figure 4—figure supplement 1I.

claim: The 26S proteasome is normally present in excess.
source: This suggests that the 26S proteasome is normally present in excess.
evidence: This is an inference based on the observation that reducing PSMD2 did not affect proteasome degradation rates.

claim: Reducing PSMD2 levels resulted in a significant and reproducible 7% decrease in the rate of protein synthesis.
source: Reducing PSMD2 levels resulted in a significant and reproducible 7% decrease in the rate of protein synthesis (Figure 4G).
evidence: This is supported by protein synthesis assay data shown in Figure 4G.

claim: Even though PSMD2 knockdown did not reduce protein degradation capacity, it did trigger a reduction in protein translation.
source: Thus, even though PSMD2 knockdown did not reduce protein degradation capacity, it did trigger a reduction in protein translation (Figure 4G), a change that may contribute to lowering basal levels of proteotoxic stress.
evidence: This is supported by protein synthesis assay data shown in Figure 4G and is an inference about the mechanism.

claim: After a 20-hr treatment with bortezomib, the rate of protein degradation sharply decreased in control cells.
source: Next, we measured protein degradation and synthesis rates after a 20-hr treatment with bortezomib. The rate of protein degradation sharply decreased in control cells (Figure 4F).
evidence: This is supported by protein degradation assay data shown in Figure 4F.

claim: Transiently reducing PSMD2 strongly counteracted the inhibition of proteasome degradation by bortezomib.
source: Transiently reducing PSMD2 strongly counteracted the inhibition of proteasome degradation (Figure 4F).
evidence: This is supported by protein degradation assay data shown in Figure 4F.

claim: Following bortezomib treatment, the rate of protein synthesis sharply decreased in control cells.
source: Following bortezomib treatment, the rate of protein synthesis also sharply decreased in control cells (Figure 4G).
evidence: This is supported by protein synthesis assay data shown in Figure 4G.

claim: The drop in protein synthesis following bortezomib treatment reflects the global repression of protein synthesis that normally follows strong proteotoxic stress.
source: This drop reflects the global repression of protein synthesis that normally follows strong proteotoxic stress (Holcik and Sonenberg, 2005; Shalgi et al., 2013).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior literature.

claim: Transiently reducing PSMD2 protein levels strongly counteracted the bortezomib-mediated suppression of protein synthesis.
source: Transiently reducing PSMD2 protein levels strongly counteracted the bortezomib-mediated suppression of protein synthesis (Figure 4G).
evidence: This is supported by protein synthesis assay data shown in Figure 4G.

claim: Reducing PSMD2 levels counteracts the effects of bortezomib on both protein degradation and protein synthesis.
source: Thus, reducing PSMD2 levels counteracts the effects of bortezomib on both protein degradation and protein synthesis.
evidence: This is a summary inference based on the protein degradation and synthesis assay data.

claim: Human cancer cell lines have a broad range of sensitivities to proteasome inhibition.
source: Human cancer cell lines have a broad range of sensitivities to proteasome inhibition.
evidence: This is established knowledge about cancer cell line drug responses.

claim: The Genomics of Drug Sensitivity in Cancer (GDSC) database contains transcriptional data and drug responsiveness collected from a spectrum of human cancer cell lines.
source: We analyzed the Genomics of Drug Sensitivity in Cancer (GDSC) database, a public resource of transcriptional data and drug responsiveness collected from a spectrum of human cancer cell lines with diverse tissue origins and diverse oncogenic lesions (Garnett et al., 2012).
evidence: This describes the data source used for analysis and is supported by citation.

claim: There was no significant difference in the average expression of 20S subunits between cells most resistant and most sensitive to MG132 or bortezomib.
source: We found no significant difference in the average expression of 20S subunits between the two groups (Figure 5A,B left panels).
evidence: This is supported by analysis of GDSC database shown in Figure 5A,B.

claim: Cells that were the most resistant to either MG132 or to bortezomib had significantly lower levels of 19S transcripts than cells that were sensitive.
source: However, cells that were the most resistant to either MG132 or to bortezomib had significantly lower levels of 19S transcripts (PSMC and PSMD mRNA) than cells that were sensitive (Figure 5A,B right panels; p-value = 0.003 for MG132; p-value = 0.0008 for bortezomib).
evidence: This is supported by analysis of GDSC database shown in Figure 5A,B.

claim: The expression levels of all proteasome subunits, both 20S and 19S, are regulated by similar mechanisms and are normally highly correlated.
source: This observation is striking as the expression levels of all proteasome subunits, both 20S and 19S, are regulated by similar mechanisms and are normally highly correlated (Jansen et al., 2002; Radhakrishnan et al., 2010, 2014; Sha and Goldberg, 2014).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior literature.

claim: Bortezomib-sensitive cells commonly showed increased expression of many different 19S subunits.
source: A heat map of genes with significantly altered expression (>twofold deviation from average) revealed that bortezomib-sensitive cells commonly showed increased expression of many different 19S subunits (Figure 5C, right panel-red).
evidence: This is supported by heat map analysis of GDSC database shown in Figure 5C.

claim: Resistant cells generally had at least a twofold reduction in expression of one or more 19S subunits.
source: Resistant cells generally had at least a twofold reduction in expression of one or more 19S subunits (Figure 5C, left panel-green).
evidence: This is supported by heat map analysis of GDSC database shown in Figure 5C.

claim: Alterations in 19S subunit expression commonly occur in the evolution of cancer cells.
source: Thus, alterations in 19S subunit expression commonly occur in the evolution of cancer cells.
evidence: This is an inference based on the analysis of cancer cell line expression data.

claim: Human cancers are increasingly viewed as complex ecosystems comprised of cells harboring enormous genetic, functional and phenotypic heterogeneity.
source: Human cancers are increasingly viewed as complex ecosystems comprised of cells harboring enormous genetic, functional and phenotypic heterogeneity (Meacham and Morrison, 2013).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to prior literature.

claim: Two cell lines were created—one expressing red fluorescent protein and doxycycline-inducible PSMD2-targeting shRNA and another expressing green fluorescent protein and a doxycycline-inducible control shRNA.
source: We created two cell lines—one line that expresses red fluorescent protein (turboRFP) and the doxycycline-inducible PSMD2-targeting shRNA and another line that expresses green fluorescent protein (GFP) and a doxycycline-inducible control shRNA (Figure 6A).
evidence: This describes the experimental methodology shown in Figure 6A.

claim: In the absence of proteasome inhibitors, the initial plating ratios of cells with and without PSMD2 knockdown were maintained for 6 days.
source: In the absence of proteasome inhibitors, the initial plating ratios of these cells were maintained for 6 days (1:1, 1:2, 1:5, and 1:10) (Figure 6A).
evidence: This is supported by FACS analysis data shown in Figure 6A.

claim: Even low concentrations of bortezomib (5 nM) substantially shifted the populations of surviving cells in favor of those with reduced PSMD2.
source: In contrast, even low concentrations of bortezomib (5 nM) substantially shifted the populations of surviving cells and higher concentrations (7.5 nM and 10 nM) elicited even more substantial shifts (Figure 6A,B).
evidence: This is supported by FACS analysis and microscopy data shown in Figure 6A,B.

claim: In the presence of proteasome inhibitors, cells with modestly reduced levels of PSMD2 had a strong competitive advantage.
source: In the presence of proteasome inhibitors, cells with modestly reduced levels of PSMD2 had a strong competitive advantage.
evidence: This is an inference based on the population shift data shown in Figure 6.

claim: The essential role of the proteasome in maintaining protein homeostasis is conserved across all eukaryotes.
source: Finally, because the essential role of the proteasome in maintaining protein homeostasis is conserved across all eukaryotes (Hilt and Wolf, 1995)
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to prior literature.

claim: A library of hypomorphic (DAmP) alleles for essential yeast genes was utilized to test the effect of 19S subunit reduction in yeast.
source: As the 19S regulatory complex components are essential for viability in yeast, we utilized a library of hypomorphic (DAmP) alleles for essential yeast genes. In this library, the expression of individual mRNA species is reduced from two to 10-fold by replacing the mRNA's 3′ untranslated region (Breslow et al., 2008).
evidence: This describes the experimental methodology and is supported by citation.

claim: DAmP-strains for 12 genes comprising the 19S regulatory complex showed no significant growth-impairment under basal conditions.
source: DAmP-strains were available for 12 genes comprising the 19S regulatory complex. These strains showed no significant growth-impairment under basal conditions (Figure 7—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is supported by yeast growth data shown in Figure 7—figure supplement 1.

claim: Five of twelve yeast 19S DAmP strains had significantly increased resistance to proteasome inhibition by MG132.
source: However, five of these twelve strains had significantly increased resistance to proteasome inhibition by MG132 (Figure 7).
evidence: This is supported by yeast growth data in the presence of MG132 shown in Figure 7.

claim: Rpn5 and Rpt6, the yeast orthologs of PSMD12 and PSMC5, were the most notable strains showing increased resistance to MG132.
source: Most notable were Rpn5 and Rpt6, the yeast orthologs of PSMD12 and PSMC5—the two most significantly enriched genes in our MG132 screen in human cells (Figure 1C).
evidence: This is supported by yeast growth data shown in Figure 7 and comparison to human screen results in Figure 1C.

claim: Shifts in the ratio of 20S/26S proteasome complexes have not previously been shown to protect cells from inhibition of flux through the proteasome.
source: While changes in the ratio of 20S/26S proteasomes have not previously been shown to protect cells from inhibition of flux through the proteasome, it is well documented that they occur.
evidence: This is a statement about the novelty of the findings relative to prior literature.

claim: A broad range of genetic, metabolic, and environmental factors can elicit changes in the 20S/26S proteasome ratio.
source: Indeed, a broad range of genetic, metabolic, and environmental factors can elicit such changes.
evidence: This is established knowledge about proteasome regulation.

claim: In human stem cells, manipulation of just a single subunit of the 19S regulatory complex modified the 20S/26S proteasome ratio.
source: In human stem cells, manipulation of just a single subunit of the 19S regulatory complex modified the 20S/26S proteasome ratio (Vilchez et al., 2012).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to prior literature.

claim: In cancer cells, many chromosomal regions are recurrently lost, and these often harbor genes that encode 19S subunits.
source: In cancer cells, many chromosomal regions are recurrently lost, and these often harbor genes that encode 19S subunits (Nijhawan et al., 2012; Davoli et al., 2013).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior literature.

claim: Nutrient depravation in yeast can increase the levels of 20S proteasome complexes.
source: For example, nutrient depravation in yeast (Bajorek et al., 2003)
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to prior literature.

claim: The activation of glutamate receptor signaling in neurons can increase the levels of 20S proteasome complexes.
source: the activation of glutamate receptor signaling in neurons (Tai et al., 2010)
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to prior literature.

claim: Mitochondrial dysfunction in yeast and mammalian cells can increase the levels of 20S proteasome complexes.
source: mitochondrial dysfunction in yeast and mammalian cells (Livnat-Levanon et al., 2014)
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to prior literature.

claim: Various states of increased oxidative stress can increase the levels of 20S proteasome complexes.
source: and various states of increased oxidative stress (Wang et al., 2010; Livnat-Levanon et al., 2014) can all increase the levels of 20S proteasome complexes.
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior literature.

claim: The ratio of proteasomes can be regulated by cellular levels of NADH, a co-enzyme that directly binds 19S subunits and influences 26S proteasome stability.
source: The ratio of proteasomes can also be regulated by cellular levels of NADH, a co-enzyme that directly binds 19S subunits and influences 26S proteasome stability (Tsvetkov et al., 2014).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to prior literature.

claim: The proteasome ratio is shifted by post-translational modifications mediated by NAD+ ADP-ribosyltransferases.
source: Further, the ratio is shifted by post-translational modifications mediated by NAD+ ADP-ribosyltransferases (Ullrich et al., 1999; Cho-Park and Steller, 2013).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior literature.

claim: The modest reductions in 19S subunits did not reduce the overall rates of protein degradation and did not activate proteotoxic stress responses suggesting that these cells normally have a buffer, or excess, of 26S proteasomes.
source: The modest reductions in 19S subunits in our experiments did not reduce the overall rates of protein degradation and did not activate proteotoxic stress responses suggesting that these cells normally have a buffer, or excess, of 26S proteasomes.
evidence: This is an inference based on the experimental observations of maintained degradation rates and lack of stress response activation.

claim: A buffer of 26S proteasomes has been recently described in neurons.
source: Such a buffer has been recently described in neurons (Asano et al., 2015)
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to prior literature.

claim: 20S proteasome complexes are highly effective in degrading oxidized proteins in an ubiquitin-independent manner.
source: These complexes are highly effective in degrading oxidized (Reinheckel et al., 1998; Grune et al., 2003) and intrinsically disordered proteins (Baugh et al., 2009; Tsvetkov et al., 2009a; Wiggins et al., 2011; Ben-Nissan and Sharon, 2014) in an ubiquitin-independent manner.
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior literature.

claim: 20S proteasome complexes are highly effective in degrading intrinsically disordered proteins in an ubiquitin-independent manner.
source: These complexes are highly effective in degrading oxidized (Reinheckel et al., 1998; Grune et al., 2003) and intrinsically disordered proteins (Baugh et al., 2009; Tsvetkov et al., 2009a; Wiggins et al., 2011; Ben-Nissan and Sharon, 2014) in an ubiquitin-independent manner.
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior literature.

claim: 20S proteasomes mediate the endoproteolytic cleavage of translation initiating factors eIF4G1, eIF4F, and eIF3a.
source: First, these complexes mediate the endoproteolytic cleavage of translation initiating factors eIF4G1, eIF4F, and eIF3a (Baugh and Pilipenko, 2004)
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to prior literature.

claim: The endoproteolytic cleavage of translation factors by 20S proteasomes could directly contribute to the inhibition of protein synthesis that occurs following 19S subunit reduction.
source: which could directly contribute to the inhibition of protein synthesis that occurs following 19S subunit reduction.
evidence: This is a speculative inference about a potential mechanism.

claim: 20S proteasomes preferentially degrade newly synthesized substrates.
source: Second, 20S proteasomes preferentially degrade newly synthesized substrates (Tsvetkov et al., 2009b; Adler et al., 2010).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior literature.

claim: 20S proteasome complexes degrade numerous intrinsically disordered proteins involved in cell cycle regulation, cell cycle control, and oncogenesis.
source: In addition, 20S proteasome complexes degrade numerous intrinsically disordered proteins involved in cell cycle regulation, cell cycle control, and oncogenesis (Asher et al., 2006; Jariel-Encontre et al., 2008; Ben-Nissan and Sharon, 2014).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior literature.

claim: The degradation of 20S substrates could underlie the robust anti-proliferation response that follows bortezomib treatment of cells with reduced 19S subunits.
source: The degradation of such 20S substrates could underlie the robust anti-proliferation response that follows bortezomib treatment of cells with reduced 19S subunits.
evidence: This is a speculative inference about a potential mechanism.

claim: A shift into a quiescent-like state likely triggers adaptive cytoprotection.
source: Such a shift into a quiescent-like state likely triggers adaptive cytoprotection.
evidence: This is a speculative inference about the protective mechanism.

claim: In yeast stationary phase, there is a reversible reduction in protein translation.
source: This is reminiscent of yeast that transition into stationary phase when nutrients are exhausted. In this setting, there is also a reversible reduction in protein translation (Fuge et al., 1994)
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to prior literature.

claim: In yeast stationary phase, levels of 26S proteasomes sharply decrease in favor of active 20S proteasomes, which are essential for viability during prolonged periods of nutrient depravation.
source: and levels of 26S proteasomes sharply decrease in favor of active 20S proteasomes, which are essential for viability during prolonged periods of nutrient depravation (Bajorek et al., 2003).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to prior literature.

claim: The protective mechanism that is generated upon 20S formation is likely conserved from yeast to human and may be part of the natural transitions used to established stress-resistant quiescent states.
source: Thus, the protective mechanism that is generated upon 20S formation is likely conserved from yeast to human and may be part of the natural transitions used to established stress-resistant quiescent states.
evidence: This is an inference based on the conservation of the mechanism and comparison to yeast biology.

claim: In nature, mechanisms for rebalancing the 20S/26S proteasome ratio most likely emerged to help cells contend with perturbations that cause protein misfolding.
source: In our experiments, this mechanism for increasing resistance was revealed by the use of highly controllable chemical compounds. However, in nature, mechanisms for rebalancing the 20S/26S proteasome ratio most likely emerged to help cells contend with perturbations that cause protein misfolding.
evidence: This is a speculative inference about the evolutionary origin of the mechanism.

claim: Intracellular and environmental insults that generate large protein aggregates are known to impair the proteolytic function of the proteasome.
source: In fact, intracellular and environmental insults that generate large protein aggregates are known to impair the proteolytic function of the proteasome (Deriziotis et al., 2011; Ayyadevara et al., 2015).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior literature.

claim: Selective pressures from naturally occurring proteasome inhibitors could have shaped the evolution of this ancient survival mechanism.
source: Such mechanisms may have also helped organisms withstand naturally occurring 20S proteasome inhibitors that are elaborated by microorganisms cohabiting their niches (Schneekloth and Crews, 2011). Such selective pressures could have shaped the evolution of this ancient survival mechanism, one that emerged long before the advent of the use of proteasome inhibitors as anti-cancer therapeutics.
evidence: This is a speculative inference about evolutionary pressures and is supported by citation.

claim: Breslow et al. found that reducing 19S subunits can rescue yeast strains that are growth inhibited by reductions in 20S subunits.
source: In agreement with our results indicating that yeast cells are protected from proteasome inhibitors by reducing 19S subunits, Breslow et al. found that reducing 19S subunits can rescue yeast strains that are growth inhibited by reductions in 20S subunits (Breslow et al., 2008).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to prior literature.

claim: Suppressing the expression of many different 19S subunits provided resistance to proteasome inhibitors.
source: Suppressing the expression of many different 19S subunits provided resistance to proteasome inhibitors and there are many potential routes for suppressing their expression (e.g., genetic, metabolic, epigenetic, environmental).
evidence: This is a summary of the experimental findings.

claim: Large populations of cells might harbor functional heterogeneity for surviving altered flux through the proteasome.
source: This raises the intriguing possibility that large populations of cells might harbor functional heterogeneity for surviving altered flux through the proteasome.
evidence: This is a speculative inference based on the findings.

claim: Some cells might be highly proliferative yet highly sensitive to proteasome inhibition, while other cells could be slowly proliferative yet highly resistant to proteasome inhibition.
source: At one extreme, some cells might be highly proliferative yet highly sensitive to proteasome inhibition, while at the other extreme, some cells could be slowly proliferative yet highly resistant to proteasome inhibition.
evidence: This is a speculative inference about cellular heterogeneity.

claim: Slowly proliferative cells with reduced 19S expression would have generally reduced relative fitness, analogous to drug-tolerant 'persister' cells that reside within tumor populations.
source: Because of their slower proliferation capacity, the latter would have generally reduced relative fitness, analogous to the small populations of drug-tolerant 'persister' cells that reside within tumor populations (Sharma et al., 2010; Glickman and Sawyers, 2012; Knoechel et al., 2014).
evidence: This is a speculative inference supported by citations to prior literature on persister cells.
